concepts.explain: In lj units everything is dimensionless: distances are multiples of sigma, energies multiples of epsilon. Nothing is in angstroms or kcal/mol.
Every atom carries a numeric type. Force field parameters are assigned per type, not per atom, so the type is what decides how an atom behaves.
A region is a named shape in space. The simulation box is built from a region, and only once the box exists can atoms exist.
An integer fixing the random sequence. The same seed reproduces a run exactly; change it for a statistically independent repeat.
Beyond the cutoff the pair interaction is simply not computed. Too short clips the attractive well; too long spends compute on forces near zero.
Parameters for unlike pairs are derived from the like pairs, by default as geometric means, so you rarely write them out yourself.
Every fix reads the same way: an ID you choose, the group it acts on, then the style and its arguments.
The integrator advances time in discrete jumps. Each must be short compared with the fastest motion, or the integration goes unstable.
LAMMPS prints a line of thermodynamic data every so many steps, and the GUI charts whichever columns you ask for.
A named subset of the atoms. Groups can be built from types, regions, or set operations on other groups, and most commands act on one.
A text file holding the box, the atoms and their parameters. Writing one lets a later run start from this state instead of rebuilding it.
An expression evaluated during the run that returns a single number, so it can be printed alongside the thermo output.
A compute calculates nothing on its own. Something has to reference it -- another compute, a fix, or a thermo_style column -- before it runs.

steps.title: Choose the rules of the world
steps.teach:
A LAMMPS script is read strictly top to bottom, and order matters: some commands only work *before* the simulation box exists, others only after. The script is laid out in five labelled sections and filled in turn.

This first section sets the global choices. None of these four are strictly required -- each matches a LAMMPS default -- but writing them down means the next person to read your script does not have to know what the defaults are.

commands.explain: Work in reduced units, where the Lennard-Jones parameters are defined as 1.

notes.alternatives: `real` gives angstroms and kcal/mol, `metal` angstroms and eV. This changes the meaning of every number below it.

commands.explain: Simulate in three dimensions.

notes.alternatives: `2` confines atoms to the xy-plane, which makes for cheap visual demonstrations.

commands.explain: The simplest particle: a point with a mass and a type.

notes.alternatives: `charge` adds a per-atom charge, `molecular` adds bonds and molecule IDs. Pick the cheapest style that holds what you need.

commands.explain: Periodic in all three directions: an atom leaving one face re-enters through the opposite one.

notes.note: the x direction, then y, then z
notes.alternatives: `f` is a fixed wall, `s` shrink-wraps to the atoms, `m` shrink-wraps with a minimum. A slab geometry would use `p p f`.

steps.title: A box, and atoms in it
steps.teach:
A *region* is only a shape; the simulation box is built from it, and only then can atoms exist.

This tutorial simulates a binary mixture: 1500 small atoms of type 1 and 100 larger ones of type 2, dropped in at random.

commands.explain: A cube 40 units on a side, centred on the origin, named simbox.

notes.alternatives: `sphere`, `cylinder` and `prism` are also available, and regions combine with union and intersect. You will use a cylinder in the second half of this tutorial.

notes.note: the six bounds, as xlo xhi ylo yhi zlo zhi
notes.alternatives: Shrinking the box at a fixed atom count raises the density.

commands.explain: Build the box from that region, with room for two atom types.

notes.note: how many atom types will ever exist
notes.alternatives: Locked in from here. Referring to a type 3 later is an error, and every type declared needs a mass and pair parameters.

commands.explain: Drop 1500 atoms of type 1 into the box at random positions.

notes.alternatives: Change it for a different arrangement of the same system.

Without it two atoms can land almost on top of each other. The Lennard-Jones repulsion goes as 1/r^12, so that produces an enormous force -- exactly the instability you will trigger deliberately later.

commands.explain: Add 100 atoms of the heavier second type, with a different seed so they land elsewhere.

steps.title: Masses, and how atoms feel each other
steps.teach:
Nothing can be computed until every atom type has a mass and every pair of types knows how to interact.

The Lennard-Jones potential is `4*eps*[(sig/r)^12 - (sig/r)^6]`. The 12 term is the hard repulsion at close range; the 6 term is the weak long-range attraction that lets a fluid condense instead of dispersing.

commands.explain: Type 1 is the light species.
Type 2 is five times heavier, so at the same temperature it moves more sluggishly.
All pairs interact through a truncated Lennard-Jones potential.

notes.alternatives: `lj/cut/coul/long` adds long-range electrostatics, `eam` is for metals. This one line decides the physics.
2.5 is the more common convention in the literature; 4.0 keeps more of the attractive tail.

commands.explain: Epsilon and sigma for a type 1 atom meeting another type 1 atom.

notes.note: epsilon, the depth of the potential well
notes.alternatives: A larger epsilon means a stronger attraction and a fluid that condenses more readily.

notes.note: sigma, the distance where the energy crosses zero
notes.alternatives: Roughly the atom's diameter. There is no default for either: lj/cut requires both.

commands.explain: The heavy species: a shallower well but a much larger diameter.

notes.alternatives: You never write a 1-2 line. LAMMPS mixes it: eps_12 = sqrt(1.0 x 0.5) = 0.707, sigma_12 = sqrt(1.0 x 3.0) = 1.732. `pair_modify` chooses another rule.

steps.title: Ask for output, then compute once
steps.teach: `run 0` initialises forces and energies without advancing time at all. It is the cheapest possible check that the system is complete and self-consistent.

commands.explain: Print a line of thermodynamic data every 10 steps.

notes.alternatives: Larger values print less. This run is short, so keep it frequent.

commands.explain: Report the step number, the total energy, and the pressure.

notes.alternatives: `temp`, `pe` and `ke` are the other common ones. Whatever you list here is what the Charts window can plot.

commands.explain: Compute forces and energy once, without taking a single timestep.

notes.alternatives: Leaving it out prints the usual timing and statistics block, which is noise for a zero-step run.

steps.title: Run it
steps.teach: Your system is complete: a box, atoms, masses and interactions. Run it once to confirm LAMMPS agrees.
steps.expect: no error, and a single line of output at step 0

steps.title: The first number
steps.teach:
The total energy at step 0 is large and **positive**.

That is expected, and it is the whole reason the next act exists. The atoms were placed at random; `overlap 0.3` prevented the very worst contacts, but 0.3 is still well inside sigma for the heavy species, so plenty of pairs sit on the steep repulsive wall where the 1/r^12 term dominates.
steps.call_to_action: Look at the etotal column in the Output window.

steps.title: Relax the structure
steps.teach:
Rather than start dynamics from a bad configuration, slide the atoms downhill into a nearby local minimum first.

LAMMPS stops when any one of four criteria is met, in this order: an energy tolerance, a force tolerance, a maximum number of iterations, and a maximum number of force evaluations. It then reports which one it was.

commands.explain: Iterate downhill until one of the four stopping criteria is met.

notes.note: energy tolerance, force tolerance, max iterations, max evaluations
notes.alternatives: Minimization finds a *local* minimum, never the global one. For anything but a trivial system there is no way to reach the global minimum this way.

steps.title: Watch it fall
steps.teach: Delete the `run 0 post no` line first -- it has done its job -- then run again.
steps.expect: the potential energy dropping quickly and then levelling off

steps.title: Positive to negative
steps.teach:
The sign change is the whole story. The atoms started jammed against each other and have moved to comfortable separations near the bottom of the Lennard-Jones well.

During minimization there is no kinetic energy at all -- nothing is moving, atoms are simply relocated downhill -- so the total energy *is* the potential energy.
steps.call_to_action: Look at the energy curve in the Charts window.
steps.expect: energy crossing from positive to negative and flattening

steps.title: See the system
steps.teach: The atoms are visibly clumping together rather than sitting on a random scatter. This is your system, rendered by LAMMPS itself from the state you just produced.
steps.call_to_action: Open the Image Viewer from the Run menu.
steps.expect: atoms gathered into contact rather than spread at random

steps.title: Let go
steps.teach:
Nothing moves in LAMMPS unless a *fix* makes it move. `fix nve` integrates Newton's equations with the velocity-Verlet algorithm and adds nothing else.

With periodic boundaries and no thermostat, this samples the microcanonical (NVE) ensemble: constant number of particles, volume and energy.

commands.explain: Report less often: this run is far longer than the minimization.

commands.text: thermo_style custom step temp etotal pe ke press
commands.explain: Once atoms move there is a temperature and a kinetic energy worth watching, and pe + ke = etotal.
Integrate every atom's motion, every step.

notes.note: an ID you choose, used later to modify or delete this fix

notes.alternatives: `all` is a default group containing every atom. Your own groups let you thermostat only part of a system.
`nvt` adds a thermostat and holds temperature instead of energy; `npt` also controls pressure.

commands.explain: Advance time in steps of 0.005 reduced time units.

notes.note: how far time moves each step
notes.alternatives: Raise this too far and the integrator steps an atom straight through its neighbour's repulsive core. Try 0.05 later and watch the total energy diverge -- it is the most common failure in molecular dynamics, and worth causing once on purpose.

commands.explain: 125 reduced time units of dynamics.

steps.title: Run the dynamics
steps.teach: The system starts far from equilibrium: the minimized structure has no thermal motion at all, so the atoms accelerate down the potential gradients.
steps.expect: potential energy falling while kinetic energy climbs, both levelling off

steps.title: Nobody chose that temperature
steps.teach:
Both energies plateau and the total fluctuates around a constant. That fluctuation, rather than a steady climb, is what a healthy NVE run looks like.

The temperature settles near 1.5. Nobody chose that: it is whatever the potential energy released happens to produce. Choosing it is what a thermostat is for.
steps.call_to_action: Switch the Charts window between etotal, pe and ke.
steps.expect: a flat total energy with pe and ke trading against each other

steps.title: A second script
steps.teach:
That script built a system and equilibrated it, but it rebuilds everything from scratch every time you run it.

The rest of this tutorial works on two further files that came with the download. The first, now open, is the same script with an empty System definition section -- you are going to fill it differently.
steps.call_to_action: Read the sections that are already filled in.

steps.title: Place the two species apart
steps.teach: Instead of mixing the species at random, put each in its own region: type 2 inside a cylinder, type 1 outside it. Watching them mix afterwards is far more informative than watching an already-mixed system stay mixed.

commands.explain: The same box as before.
Two atom types again.

commands.text: region cyl_in cylinder z 0 0 10 INF INF side in
commands.explain: The inside of a cylinder of radius 10, running the full height of the box along z.

notes.alternatives: `x` or `y` would orient it differently. The two INF values run it the full length of the box.

notes.note: which side of the surface counts as the region
notes.alternatives: `side out` is the complement -- everything in the box that is *not* in the cylinder. The next line uses exactly that.

commands.text: region cyl_out cylinder z 0 0 10 INF INF side out
commands.explain: Everything outside the same cylinder.
1000 light atoms, placed only outside the cylinder.
150 heavy atoms, placed only inside it.

steps.title: Save the result
steps.teach: A sixth section, after the minimization. Writing the state to a data file means the next script can start from it rather than repeating the setup and the minimization.

commands.explain: Write the box, the atoms, their types and positions, and the pair coefficients to a text file.

notes.alternatives: `write_restart` writes a binary file instead: smaller, faster, and it records the atom and pair styles too -- but it is not portable between LAMMPS versions or platforms, which is why a data file is used here.

steps.title: Build and save
steps.teach: This run creates the file the next script reads.

steps.title: The third script
steps.teach:
This one holds only the Initialization section. Everything else comes from the data file you just wrote.

One ordering catch: `pair_style` must now come **before** the box exists, which means before `read_data`. The data file carries the coefficients but not the style.

steps.title: Read the saved system
steps.teach: Two lines replace the whole System definition and Settings sections of the first script.

commands.explain: The style must be set before the box is created.
Rebuild the box, the atoms, the masses and the pair coefficients from the file.

steps.title: Clean up the misplaced atoms
steps.teach:
Minimization moved some atoms across the cylinder wall, so the starting state is not quite clean. Rebuild the two regions -- regions are not saved in a data file -- then use groups to find the atoms on the wrong side and delete them.

Groups are built from types, from regions, and from set operations on other groups. That composability is the point.

commands.text: region cyl_in cylinder z 0 0 10 INF INF side in
commands.explain: Regions are not stored in a data file, so they have to be defined again.

commands.text: region cyl_out cylinder z 0 0 10 INF INF side out
commands.explain: And the complement.
Every atom of type 1.

notes.alternatives: `region` selects by position, `id` by atom number, `union`/`intersect`/`subtract` combine existing groups.

commands.explain: Every atom of type 2.
Every atom currently inside the cylinder.

notes.note: membership is evaluated now, not continuously
notes.alternatives: The group keeps the atoms it matched when this line ran, even after they move. That is what makes the deletion below well defined.

commands.explain: Every atom currently outside it.
Light atoms that drifted inside -- the ones that do not belong.
Heavy atoms that drifted outside.
Remove them, leaving a clean starting arrangement.
And the same on the other side.

steps.title: Measure the mixing
steps.teach:
Now the interesting part: measure how the two species mix, rather than just watching them.

Two equal-style variables count the atoms of each type still inside the cylinder. Two computes measure the coordination number -- how many type 2 atoms sit near each type 1 atom -- and average it, which is a good scalar indicator of how mixed the system is.

commands.explain: How many light atoms are inside the cylinder right now.

notes.alternatives: `equal` returns one number evaluated during the run. Other styles include `atom`, `index`, `loop`, `file` and `vector`.

commands.explain: And how many heavy atoms.

commands.text: compute coor12 grp_t1 coord/atom cutoff 2 group grp_t2
commands.explain: For each type 1 atom, count the type 2 atoms within 2 length units.

notes.alternatives: The suffix tells you what it produces: no suffix is global data, `/atom` per-atom, `/local` local, `/chunk` per-chunk. This one is per-atom, so something has to reduce it before it can be printed.

commands.text: compute sumcoor12 grp_t1 reduce ave c_coor12
commands.explain: Average that per-atom count over all type 1 atoms, giving a single number.

notes.alternatives: The `c_` prefix means "the output of compute coor12". Without a consumer like this, the first compute would never be evaluated at all.

steps.title: Run it, and print the measurements
steps.teach: Give the atoms an initial temperature, thermostat them, and report the two variables and the averaged coordination alongside the usual columns.

commands.text: thermo_style custom step temp etotal v_n1_in v_n2_in c_sumcoor12
commands.explain: The `v_` and `c_` prefixes pull in your variables and your compute.

commands.text: velocity all create 1.0 49284 mom yes dist gaussian
commands.explain: Start every atom moving, drawn from a Gaussian at temperature 1.0, with zero net momentum.

notes.alternatives: Without `mom yes` the whole system can drift bodily across the box, which contributes to the temperature without meaning anything.

commands.explain: Integrate the motion.

commands.text: fix mylgv all langevin 1.0 1.0 0.1 10917 zero yes
commands.explain: Hold the temperature at 1.0 with friction and random kicks.

notes.note: temperature at the start of the run, then at the end
notes.alternatives: Making them differ ramps the temperature over the run, which is how you heat or quench a system.
Smaller values couple more strongly and disturb the dynamics more; larger ones equilibrate more slowly.

notes.note: keep the random forces from adding net momentum

commands.explain: The same stable timestep as before.
Long enough to watch the two species genuinely mix.

steps.title: Watch them mix
steps.teach: This is the longest run in the tutorial. You are now measuring something, not just simulating it.
steps.expect: n1_in rising and n2_in falling as the species interdiffuse

steps.title: The measurement, not the picture
steps.teach:
`n1_in` climbs as light atoms wander into the cylinder and `n2_in` falls as heavy ones leave. The averaged coordination number rises towards a plateau: that plateau is the mixed state.

This is the difference between watching a simulation and doing science with one. The picture is suggestive; the curve is evidence.
steps.call_to_action: Select each column in turn in the Charts window.
steps.expect: the coordination number rising and flattening as mixing completes

steps.title: It is yours now
steps.teach:
Three things worth trying, all one number each:

**Raise the timestep** to 0.05 and re-run. The total energy climbs without bound and the run may stop with **ERROR: Lost atoms** -- the integrator has stepped an atom through its neighbour's repulsive core. It almost never means atoms were really lost; it means the integration went unstable.

**Deepen the heavy-atom well** with `pair_coeff 2 2 2.0 3.0` and see whether the species separate again instead of mixing.

**Ramp the temperature** by giving `fix langevin` different start and end values.

Every run here is deliberately short enough to finish on a laptop, and none of them is long enough for statistically meaningful results.
steps.call_to_action: Change something and run it again.
